sourceChecks.claim: Live Gilbert/Lynch paper defines the asynchronous distributed read/write model and proves no implementation guarantees both atomic consistency and availability under lost communication.
Live Gilbert/Lynch partition model allows arbitrary cross-component message loss without requiring crashed nodes. Tolerance does not assert both availability and consistency.

Live Gilbert/Lynch section 2.1 defines linearizability and explicitly requires later reads to reflect completed writes or later writes; the single order respects real time rather than synchronized timestamps.

Live Gilbert/Lynch section 2.2 requires every request at non-failing nodes to terminate, with no practical time bound; its read/write proof requires valid operation responses, not a service-unavailable substitute.
Live Gilbert/Lynch proof composes isolated write and read executions; the reader cannot distinguish an unseen write from no write, so guessing cannot guarantee the correct value.

Live Raft paper describes replicated-log commitment after majority replication and safety across terms. The deck explicitly assumes a majority agreement protocol, so connected 2-of-3 can continue while 1-of-3 cannot commit alone.

Live Eric Brewer retrospective discusses partition operation and recovery, preserving invariants and reconciling conflicting histories. Continued local availability does not inherently preserve all accepted intent.

Live DynamoDB read consistency distinguishes eventual reads that can miss recent writes from optional strong reads and deployment-specific global modes. Brewer recovery discussion supplies reconciliation context; neither defines a universal deadline or lossless conflict policy.

Live Brewer retrospective rejects an unconditional two-of-three reading and discusses operation/data-specific partition management and recovery. Practical latency and cost require additional analysis beyond the theorem.
